displayQuote: Who are you going to believe, me or your own eyes?

meta.title: Who really said "Who are you going to believe, me or your own eyes?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: A Duck Soup line — but Chico Marx says it, not Groucho, and the screenplay is by Bert Kalmar and Harry Ruby. The Groucho credit dates to 1997.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Who are you going to believe, me or your own eyes?'?
meta.ogDescription: Right film, wrong brother. Chico says it in Duck Soup (1933) while disguised as Groucho’s character — which is exactly why the mix-up happened.

answer.label: Not Groucho Marx — spoken by Chico, written by Bert Kalmar and Harry Ruby
answer.authorDates: Screenwriters · credited with the screenplay of Duck Soup (1933)
answer.sourceLine: The film is right and the brother is wrong. Wikiquote’s transcription of Duck Soup ↗ gives the exchange as “Mrs. Teasdale: But I saw you with my own eyes! / Chicolini: [in disguise as Rufus T. Firefly] Well, who you gonna believe, me or your own eyes?” Chicolini is played by Chico Marx ↗; the joke of the scene is that he is impersonating Groucho’s character, which is very likely why the line has ended up filed under Groucho’s name. Quote Investigator ↗ reaches the same conclusion and finds no Groucho attribution before 1997.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Bert Kalmar and Harry Ruby, with additional dialogue by Arthur Sheekman and Nat Perrin; directed by Leo McCarey
Chicolini (Chico Marx), disguised as Rufus T. Firefly — a fictional character — to Mrs. Gloria Teasdale (Margaret Dumont)
Groucho Marx, usually in the form “me or your lying eyes”

source.excerpt:
Mrs. Teasdale: But I saw you with my own eyes!
Chicolini: [in disguise as Rufus T. Firefly] Well, who you gonna believe, me or your own eyes?
trail: Wikiquote’s Duck Soup page ↗ transcribes the exchange in its Dialogue section and attributes the line to Chicolini, with the stage direction “in disguise as Rufus T. Firefly”. The same page’s header records the credits: directed by Leo McCarey, written by Bert Kalmar and Harry Ruby.

Quote Investigator ↗ opens its article by stating that the remark “was spoken by Chico Marx who was playing the character Chicolini” and gives its own transcription of the same exchange with Margaret Dumont. It notes explicitly that Chico “was imitating the appearance of the character played by Groucho Marx causing other members of the cast to confuse their identities”.

QI dates the Groucho attribution and finds it very late: a lawyer’s closing argument reported in The Boston Globe of 23 January 1997 credited “Who you gonna believe, me or your lying eyes?” to Marx. Groucho died in 1977, so QI records that he “implausibly received credit by 1997” — twenty years after his death and sixty-four after the film.

Wikipedia’s article on the film ↗ confirms the credits independently: a 1933 Paramount comedy released 17 November 1933, “written by Bert Kalmar and Harry Ruby (with additional dialogue by Arthur Sheekman and Nat Perrin) and directed by Leo McCarey”, starring all four Marx brothers with Margaret Dumont.
source.excerptNote: Note the wording. The film has “Well, who you gonna believe”; the popular version smooths this to “Who are you going to believe”, and a second, even more widespread variant replaces “your own eyes” with “your lying eyes” — a phrase that, per Quote Investigator, does not attach to this joke until the 1970s, decades after the film.

sourceLink.text: Wikiquote: Duck Soup — the transcribed dialogue

source.rightsNote: Screen dialogue is work made for hire, so the rights sit with the studio rather than with Kalmar and Ruby personally. Duck Soup was released by Paramount Pictures in November 1933 — well after the 1931 line beyond which works are still protected in the United States — so the film and its dialogue remain in copyright.

author.name: Bert Kalmar and Harry Ruby
author.heading: About Bert Kalmar and Harry Ruby
author.metaLine: Songwriters and screenwriters · credited screenplay, Duck Soup (1933)
author.bio: Bert Kalmar and Harry Ruby were a Tin Pan Alley songwriting team who moved into screenwriting and wrote for the Marx Brothers at Paramount, including Horse Feathers (1932) and Duck Soup (1933). Their credit on Duck Soup is shared: Arthur Sheekman and Nat Perrin are credited with additional dialogue, and no source we have found assigns this particular line to one writer rather than another. What is documented is who says it — Chico Marx, playing Chicolini in a stolen greasepaint moustache.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The right film, the wrong brother — and a costume that explains the whole mistake.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ states the line “was spoken by Chico Marx who was playing the character Chicolini”, and Wikiquote’s transcription ↗ assigns it to Chicolini. QI dates the Groucho credit to a 1997 newspaper report — twenty years after his death.

In the scene Chicolini is impersonating Rufus T. Firefly, Chico ↗ in Groucho’s painted moustache and glasses. Anyone recalling the moment from memory remembers a man who looks exactly like Groucho saying it — which is the mix-up built into the joke.

The film says “your own eyes”. QI traces “lying eyes” to a separate line of descent — the phrase appears in a 1948 Dorothy Dix column and in a 1971 Ace Reid cartoon — and it is the “lying eyes” form that most often reaches print under Groucho’s name.

items.who: A popular song of the early 1900s
items.why: QI documents a song titled “Do You Believe Your Baby or Your Eyes” described in a Santa Cruz newspaper in 1904, and the same gag retold in 1918 and 1921. The Marx Brothers sharpened an existing joke rather than inventing one.

misattribution.truthLine: It is a real Duck Soup line, and Chico Marx ↗ delivers it — dressed as Groucho, which is exactly how the credit went astray.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line has escaped the film completely. It gets deployed in courtrooms, editorials and press briefings as the standard shorthand for a denial that contradicts the evidence in front of you — and it usually arrives with Groucho’s name attached and the word "lying" inserted. Quote Investigator’s earliest Groucho citation is itself an example: a defence lawyer using it in a closing argument in 1997.

The irony is that the scene is about exactly this. Chicolini is asking Mrs. Teasdale to disbelieve her eyes while wearing a disguise, and audiences have spent ninety years believing their memory of who was in it rather than the film.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator traces the joke back three decades before the film. A song called “Do You Believe Your Baby or Your Eyes” was in circulation by 1904, in which a young man who has seen his sweetheart with a rival is asked to choose and chooses her; the same exchange is retold as a comic letter in a South Carolina paper in 1918, and the actress Peggy Hopkins Joyce used the phrase to dodge a question about her age in 1921. Kalmar and Ruby were compressing a joke the audience already half-knew.

The “lying eyes” version has its own separate history. QI finds the concept in a 1948 Dorothy Dix advice column about a wife who would disbelieve her own eyes, the compressed phrasing in a 1971 Ace Reid cartoon about cattle thieves, and a full retelling in a Texas column in 1972 — none of them referring to the Marx Brothers at all.
context.pull: A line about distrusting your own eyes, misremembered by everyone who saw it.
